rv.q: Both harsh and heartwrenching, this is a needling play that's of its time and yet still surging with post-modern vitality.
Albee's 1967. Pulitzer Prize-winner is superbly directed by Pam MacKinnon and so well performed by a trans-Atlantic ensemble.
MacKinnon helms a lustrous cast toplined by Glenn Close and John Lithgow
If this production of “A Delicate Balance” teeters unsteadily at moments, it remains always fascinating to behold.

Things finally become interesting, even zany, in the second scene of the second act. Until then, though, “A Delicate Balance” comes across like a dramatically static rewrite of “Virginia Woolf” with rather less drinking and much less cursing."
Pam MacKinnon directs this solid revival with a keen ear for the curling, teasing rhythms of Albee’s ornate lines, and the performances are top-notch...this Pulitzer winner still stings and sings.
But they’re giving us the play, instead of living it.
As the play turns to the absurd, Albee’s writing brims with black humor and red-hot loathing.
This revival of Edward Albee's 1966. Pulitzer Prize-winning play is a masterclass in theatrical precision, with Glenn Close delivering a performance of stunning emotional complexity.
Lithgow, meantime, is riveting every moment he’s on stage — which is a lot — even when Tobias is silent.

'A Delicate Balance' is a long play, and, particularly in Agnes' lengthy speeches, it can slow down, and become gloomy. It's a pitfall that this production, which is mostly rewarding, doesn't completely avoid. Its biggest asset is Lithgow, who gives one of those masterful performances that's entertaining even as it's dramatically potent.
For those who've seen it--and much of his canon--before, this revival could feel a bit off-balance.
Her performance is also why this “Delicate Balance,” directed by Pam Mackinnon, is blunt and unsubtle.
Despite the witty lines and a handful of exciting moments, the production is a three-hour, very static bore.
Albee’s play is a masterpiece and this group conveys it very well.
